q: How much heat should I recover from furnace flue gas, and how is the recovery rate calculated?
title: Waste heat recovery rate for furnaces
short: Waste heat recovery rate is the heat recovered divided by the sensible heat in the exhaust gas, times 100. BEE's MSME guidelines expect at least 30% from forging, aluminium and galvanizing furnaces, with targets of 38 to 49%, and flue gas leaving at 250 to 300 °C with natural draft or 150 to 250 °C with induced draft.
audience: Furnace and boiler engineers planning a recuperator, air preheater or economiser

ul: Forging furnace, exhaust 600 to 1,000 °C: standard 30%, target 49%
Heat treatment furnace, exhaust up to 600 °C: standard 30%, target 38%
Aluminium bulk melting furnace, exhaust 500 to 600 °C: standard 30%, target 49%
Galvanizing furnace, exhaust up to 600 °C: standard 30%, target 38%
Glass tank furnace, exhaust 1,200 to 1,300 °C: standard 47%, target 57%
Glass pot furnace, exhaust 800 to 1,000 °C: standard 37%, target 49%
Boiler in a chemicals or dye unit, exhaust 400 to 600 °C: standard 22%, target 43%

p: The standard assumes the top of the exhaust temperature range and a heat exchanger working at 60% efficiency. The target assumes the bottom of the range and 65% efficiency. Natural draft systems leave flue gas hotter than induced draft ones.

ul: Air preheater or recuperator: heats combustion air with flue gas
Charge preheater: heats the material going in, such as aluminium scrap, billets or glass cullet
Economiser on a boiler: heats feedwater

p: Recovery equipment fouls. BEE asks chemical and dye units to clean and maintain flue path recovery systems every six months to stop scale cutting performance.

senseible: Senseible reads fuel invoices into monthly totals, so the fuel saved after fitting a recuperator or economiser shows in the record against the months before.
